title: 484. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Infinite Sets and Countable Examples
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an infinite set of integers from a large finite one.
questions.question: Which of the following sets is infinite?

options.label: A
options.text: The set of integers from \(-1000\) to \(1000\)

options.label: B
options.text: The set of positive even integers

questions.explanation: The positive even integers \(2,4,6,\ldots\) have no largest element: for any even number \(n\), the number \(n+2\) is a larger one. So the set is infinite. The integers from \(-1000\) to \(1000\) can be counted; there are exactly \(2001\) of them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the set has a largest element that ends the listing.

questions.learningObjective: State what it means for a set to be countably infinite.
questions.question: What does it mean to say that an infinite set \(S\) is countable?

options.label: A
options.text: The set \(S\) has a largest element.

options.label: B
options.text: The elements of \(S\) can be listed as a sequence \(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\) in which every element appears.

questions.explanation: A set is countably infinite when there is a one-to-one correspondence between its elements and the positive integers, which amounts to listing all its elements in an unending sequence. Having a largest element is unrelated: the positive integers are countable and have no largest element.
questions.hint: Think of matching the elements with the positions \(1,2,3,\ldots\) of a list.

questions.learningObjective: Use an explicit correspondence to show that the positive even integers are countable.
questions.question: Is the set of positive even integers countable?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; the rule \(n\mapsto 2n\) matches each positive integer with exactly one positive even integer.

options.label: B
options.text: No; there are fewer even integers than positive integers, so they cannot be matched.

questions.explanation: The rule \(n\mapsto 2n\) sends \(1,2,3,\ldots\) to \(2,4,6,\ldots\). Different inputs give different outputs, and every positive even integer \(m\) is reached, from \(n=\frac{m}{2}\). So the correspondence is one-to-one and onto. For infinite sets, being a proper subset does not prevent such a matching.
questions.hint: Check that the rule reaches every even number and never uses one twice.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise a listing that shows the integers are countable.
questions.question: Which statement about the set \(\mathbb{Z}\) of all integers is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is not countable, because it has no smallest element to start a list.

options.label: B
options.text: It is countable; it can be listed as \(0,1,-1,2,-2,3,-3,\ldots\)

questions.explanation: The sequence \(0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots\) contains every integer exactly once: the integer \(k>0\) appears at position \(2k\), and \(-k\) at position \(2k+1\). A list does not have to follow the usual order of the numbers, so the lack of a smallest element is no obstacle.
questions.hint: A listing may arrange the elements in any order, as long as every element appears.

questions.learningObjective: Apply an explicit one-to-one correspondence between two infinite sets.
questions.question: The rule \(f(n)=2n\) matches the positive integers with the positive even integers. Which positive integer \(n\) is matched with the even number \(50\)?
questions.explanation: Solve \(2n=50\) to get \(n=25\). The number \(100\) is \(f(50)\), the even number matched with \(50\), which is the opposite direction.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise that density does not prevent countability.
questions.question: Which statement about the set \(\mathbb{Q}\) of rational numbers is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is countable, because its elements can be arranged in a single list.

options.label: B
options.text: It is uncountable, because between any two rational numbers there is another rational number.

questions.explanation: The positive rationals can be listed by going through the fractions \(\frac{p}{q}\) in order of \(p+q\) and skipping repeats: \(\frac{1}{1},\frac{1}{2},\frac{2}{1},\frac{1}{3},\frac{3}{1},\ldots\); zero and the negatives can then be interleaved. So \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable. Having another rational between any two (density) concerns the usual order, not whether a complete list exists.
questions.hint: A list of the elements need not follow their order on the number line.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a standard example of an uncountable set.
questions.question: Which of the following sets is uncountable?

options.label: A
options.text: The set \(\mathbb{Q}\) of rational numbers

options.label: B
options.text: The set \(\mathbb{R}\) of real numbers

questions.explanation: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that no sequence can contain every real number: from any proposed list a real number can be built that differs from the \(n\)th listed number in its \(n\)th decimal place. So \(\mathbb{R}\) is uncountable. The rational numbers, in contrast, can be arranged in a list and are countable.
questions.hint: Recall which number system is the subject of Cantor's diagonal argument.

questions.concept: A set matched with a proper subset
questions.learningObjective: Find a one-to-one correspondence between an infinite set and one of its proper subsets.
questions.question: Here \(\mathbb{Z}^{+}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\). Which rule is a one-to-one correspondence from \(\mathbb{Z}^{+}\) onto \(\mathbb{Z}^{+}\setminus\{1\}=\{2,3,4,\ldots\}\)?

options.label: A
options.text: \(n\mapsto 2n\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(n\mapsto n+1\)

questions.explanation: The rule \(n\mapsto n+1\) sends \(1,2,3,\ldots\) to \(2,3,4,\ldots\); it is one-to-one and reaches every integer \(m\ge 2\), from \(n=m-1\). The rule \(n\mapsto 2n\) is one-to-one but reaches only even numbers, so it misses \(3\) and is not onto \(\{2,3,4,\ldots\}\).
questions.hint: Check whether the number \(3\) is reached by each rule.

questions.concept: Position in a listing of the integers
questions.learningObjective: Locate an element in a standard listing of the integers.
questions.question: The integers are listed as \(0,1,-1,2,-2,3,-3,\ldots\). In which position does \(-3\) appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Position \(6\)

options.label: B
options.text: Position \(7\)

questions.explanation: Counting along the list: \(0\) is first, \(1\) second, \(-1\) third, \(2\) fourth, \(-2\) fifth, \(3\) sixth, and \(-3\) seventh. In general \(-k\) is in position \(2k+1\), which gives \(7\) for \(k=3\). Position \(6\) holds \(3\).
questions.hint: Write out the list far enough, or find the pattern for the positions of \(k\) and \(-k\).

questions.learningObjective: Recognise that the set of ordered pairs of positive integers is countable.
questions.question: Is the set \(\mathbb{Z}^{+}\times\mathbb{Z}^{+}\) of all ordered pairs of positive integers countable?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; the pairs can be listed in groups of constant sum: \((1,1)\), then \((1,2),(2,1)\), then \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\), and so on.

options.label: B
options.text: No; listing the pairs row by row never finishes the first row, so no list can contain them all.

questions.explanation: For each \(s\ge 2\) there are only finitely many pairs \((a,b)\) with \(a+b=s\), namely \(s-1\) of them. Listing the groups for \(s=2,3,4,\ldots\) one after another reaches every pair after finitely many steps. Listing row by row fails, but that only shows that one particular method does not work.
questions.hint: Group the pairs so that each group is finite, then list the groups in turn.
